INTRODUCTION

[1] Mr. XXXX, you, your wife and your minor children state that you are citizens of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and that you fear persecution in that country because you are a member of the XXXX and belong to the political party of former president Joseph Kabila.1

[2] Ms. XXXX, you are acting as the designated representative of your minor children. One of your daughters, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of the United States of America.

[3] Canada's Minister of Public Safety (the Minister) has intervened in your claims for refugee protection. The Minister contends that some of you are permanent residents of the United States of America and that, in general, you lack credibility.2

[4] Ms. XXXX, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) concluded that you and two of your minor children are permanent residents of the United States of America and that you are persons referred to in the exclusion clause in section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). It also determined that you, Mr. XXXX, and your minor daughter, a US citizen, are not refugees within the meaning of the Refugee Convention,3 nor persons in need of protection.4

[5] In your appeal, you are asking for an oral hearing to be held. You contend that the RPD erred in applying the exclusion clause, improperly assessed the applicability of section 96 of the IRPA, rather than section 97, and violated the provisions of sections 7 to 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Canada's international obligations.5

[6] Having conducted my analysis of your record, I conclude that it is not possible to hold an oral hearing and that the RPD did not err as alleged.

[7] In the light of those findings, your appeal is dismissed.
I. HOLDING AN ORAL HEARING BEFORE THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[8] The Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) stipulate that persons who are the subject of the appeal must include in their memorandum full and detailed submissions regarding why the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) should hold a hearing.6

[9] Your memorandum contains no submissions to that effect.

[10] In your written statement, you ask for an oral hearing to be held so that you can better explain your problems, because the RPD did not properly grasp all the facts in your record and rejected your refugee protection claims after improperly interpreting texts and your credibility.7

II. ANALYSIS OF THE APPEAL

[12] The role of the RAD is not to conduct a de novo consideration of refugee protection claims, but rather to determine whether the RPD erred as alleged.10 I conducted my own analysis of your record, which included reading the transcript of the RPD hearing,11 the documentary evidence and the applicable law. I concluded that the correctness standard of review must be applied.12
A. The errors you allege were made by the Refugee Protection Division

[13] Paragraph 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules stipulates that the person who is the subject of the appeal must specify (i) the errors that are the grounds for the appeal, and (ii) where the errors are located in the RPD's decision, in the transcript or in any recording of the hearing.13

[14] In your memorandum, you contend that the RPD erred in its decision.

[15] First, by excluding your wife and two of your minor children, with their status as permanent residents of the United States of America, despite the RPD being aware of their fear that they had lost their permanent resident status in that country because they had been away for more than six months and had not filed income tax returns. Given that doubt, the RPD should, in your opinion, find in your favour. In addition, you argue that counsel for the Minister provided no evidence that their permanent resident status in the United States was still in effect, although he was supposed to do so.14

subthemes.text:
[19] On December 22, the Chairperson of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada designated the decision by my colleague Jo-Anne Pickel in file MB8-0002518 as a jurisprudential guide. This decision provides an in-depth interpretation of Article IE of the Refugee Convention. As a jurisprudential guide, its purpose is to set out the approach that must be followed in deciding on refugee protection claims based on this issue, and appeals thereof, in order to provide some consistency in decision-making within the RPD and the RAD.19 In the rest of my own analysis, I will use the approach that the decision proposes, as needed.

[20] In its decision, the RPD analyzed your testimony20 and the documentary evidence, specifically the resident cards for your wife and two of your children. They were issued in XXXX 2017 and are valid for a period of ten years, that is, until XXXX 2027. It came to the conclusion that, on a balance of probabilities, your wife and two of your minor children, who are citizens of the DRC, are permanent residents of the United States of America, a status that guarantees them rights equivalent to those enjoyed by citizens of that country. Having analyzed the various criteria that the loss of that status in the country can entail, it concluded that, on the final day of the hearing, your wife and your two children were still permanent residents of the United States, since you did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that their status had been cancelled by the US authorities.21

[21] In its decision, the RPD then focused on the presumption that the US authorities would be willing and able to protect you. It came to the conclusion that you had not rebutted that presumption.22

[22] According to my own analysis of your record, the RPD did not err as alleged when it found, on a balance of probabilities, that your wife and two of your children were still permanent residents of the United States of America on the final day of your hearing. At that time, in my opinion, it considered the relevant facts and law.23 The onus of showing that your wife and your two children had lost that status was clearly yours, and you did not do so.24 The existence of criteria that can lead to the loss of permanent resident status does not in itself give rise to the conclusion that, as a direct result, your wife and your two children did lose their status.25

[23] I will now refer to the principles applicable to your case, using the decision by my colleague Jo-Anne Pickel as my model. This has been designated as a jurisprudential guide in the approach to the analysis of a possible exclusion pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention:
- The appropriate date for assessing an appellant's status in their country of residence for the purpose of Article 1E of the Convention is the date of the RPD hearing.26
- Consideration must be given to the risk raised by claimants in respect of their country of residence prior to concluding that they are excluded from protection by the combined effect of Article 1E of the Convention and section 98 of the IRPA.27

[24] In your memorandum, you did not challenge the appropriate date for assessing your wife's permanent resident status in the United States, and that of two of your children, as the date of the RPD hearing. Nor did you challenge the RPD's conclusion in relation to the unrebutted presumption that the US authorities would be willing and able to protect your wife and your two children.

[25] As I indicated earlier, there is no basis for the argument in your memorandum that it was up to the Minister's representative to show that your wife and your two children still had permanent resident status in the United States.

[26] The RPD concluded that your wife and two of your children are persons referred to in Article 1E of the Refugee Convention, within the meaning of section 98 of the IRPA. This was not an error, in my opinion. The RPD did not have to analyze their claims in terms of their country of citizenship, the DRC, because that section itself makes it clear that they cannot be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
Applicability of section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and your credibility

[27] In its decision, the RPD identified a number of omissions, contradictions and implausibilities, not to mention behaviour inconsistent with that of a person who is being persecuted or who fears for his life. This led it to find that you were not a credible witness.28

[28] According to my own analysis of your record, in assessing your credibility, the RPD did not focus on useless details rather than the major issues. Nor did it set traps for you with the goal of rejecting your claim for refugee protection. It did not lack impartiality.

[29] Personally, I am of the opinion that the omissions, contradictions and implausibilities that the RPD identified clearly arose from the testimony you gave at the hearing and the documentary evidence you submitted. They deal with important aspects of your refugee protection claim. Let me give you an example. You testified about allegedly being the victim of an abduction in XXXX outside the XXXX XXXX in Kinshasa, ordered by the XXXX of the OGEFREM, about the time when you allegedly filed a complaint about it with the police, and about the follow-up to that complaint. You then contradicted yourself about your use of time, in that you were either at home for XXXX days or that you were in hospital. Then you ended up stating that your father took you to the hospital after the abduction. You contradicted yourself again a few seconds later when you stated that your father insisted that the police should see what had happened to you before you arrived at the hospital.29 It is clear to me that, not only did you contradict yourself, but your testimony also clearly changed with each statement you made.

[30] According to my own analysis of your record, the RPD did not err in any way when it found that the credibility of your allegations was seriously undermined by a number of omissions, contradictions and implausibilities.
Canada's constitutional and international obligations

[31] In your memorandum, you contend that, since you have no possibility of protection from the corrupt members of public institutions in the DRC, Canada would be in clear violation of its constitutional and international obligations if the RPD's determination is confirmed. With all respect, that argument has no merit.

It must be stated at this point that neither the RPD decision, nor my own decision, are about your deportation. They are only about whether you are a refugee or a person in need of protection within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.30 In this case, I see no exceptional circumstances that would give me cause to analyze a constitutional issue.31

[32] Actually, the argument is whether your potential deportation to the DRC would violate sections 7 and 12 of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms and our international obligations. It must be stated at this point that neither the RPD decision, nor my own decision, are about your deportation. They are only about whether you are a refugee or a person in need of protection within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.30 In this case, I see no exceptional circumstances that would give me cause to analyze a constitutional issue.31

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] Mr. XXXX, you, your wife and your minor children state that you are citizens of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and that you fear persecution in that country because you are a member of the XXXX and belong to the political party of former president Joseph Kabila.1
[2] Ms. XXXX, you are acting as the designated representative of your minor children. One of your daughters, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of the United States of America.

[3] Canada's Minister of Public Safety (the Minister) has intervened in your claims for refugee protection. The Minister contends that some of you are permanent residents of the United States of America and that, in general, you lack credibility.2

[4] Ms. XXXX, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) concluded that you and two of your minor children are permanent residents of the United States of America and that you are persons referred to in the exclusion clause in section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). It also determined that you, Mr. XXXX, and your minor daughter, a US citizen, are not refugees within the meaning of the Refugee Convention,3 nor persons in need of protection.4

[5] In your appeal, you are asking for an oral hearing to be held. You contend that the RPD erred in applying the exclusion clause, improperly assessed the applicability of section 96 of the IRPA, rather than section 97, and violated the provisions of sections 7 to 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Canada's international obligations.5
[6] Having conducted my analysis of your record, I conclude that it is not possible to hold an oral hearing and that the RPD did not err as alleged.

[7] In the light of those findings, your appeal is dismissed.
I. HOLDING AN ORAL HEARING BEFORE THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[8] The Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) stipulate that persons who are the subject of the appeal must include in their memorandum full and detailed submissions regarding why the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) should hold a hearing.6
[9] Your memorandum contains no submissions to that effect.

[10] In your written statement, you ask for an oral hearing to be held so that you can better explain your problems, because the RPD did not properly grasp all the facts in your record and rejected your refugee protection claims after improperly interpreting texts and your credibility.7

[11] The onus is on the RAD to determine whether the criteria in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA have been met.8 One of the criteria in that subsection is that evidence submitted on appeal must have been found to be admissible. In your appeal, you submitted no evidence in accordance with subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. Consequently, it is not possible to hold an oral hearing.9
II. ANALYSIS OF THE APPEAL

[12] The role of the RAD is not to conduct a de novo consideration of refugee protection claims, but rather to determine whether the RPD erred as alleged.10 I conducted my own analysis of your record, which included reading the transcript of the RPD hearing,11 the documentary evidence and the applicable law. I concluded that the correctness standard of review must be applied.12
A. The errors you allege were made by the Refugee Protection Division

[13] Paragraph 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules stipulates that the person who is the subject of the appeal must specify (i) the errors that are the grounds for the appeal, and (ii) where the errors are located in the RPD's decision, in the transcript or in any recording of the hearing.13
[14] In your memorandum, you contend that the RPD erred in its decision.

[15] First, by excluding your wife and two of your minor children, with their status as permanent residents of the United States of America, despite the RPD being aware of their fear that they had lost their permanent resident status in that country because they had been away for more than six months and had not filed income tax returns. Given that doubt, the RPD should, in your opinion, find in your favour. In addition, you argue that counsel for the Minister provided no evidence that their permanent resident status in the United States was still in effect, although he was supposed to do so.14

[16] Then, you contend that the RPD failed to appreciate the possibility of analyzing your refugee protection claim under section 96 of the IRPA, given that, in your opinion, there is no difference between your membership in the political party and in the XXXX in terms of the attack by Mr. XXXX.15 As for your credibility, you argue that the RPD focused on useless details rather than on the main issues and that it should have made an effort to be impartial and to examine your record objectively.16

[17] Finally, you contend that, since you have no possibility of protection from the corrupt members of public institutions in the DRC, Canada would be in clear violation of its constitutional and international obligations if the RPD's determination is confirmed.17
B. The Refugee Protection Division did not err as alleged

[18] Having analyzed your record, I conclude that the RPD did not err as alleged. This is why.
Permanent residence in the United States for your wife and two of your children

[19] On December 22, the Chairperson of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada designated the decision by my colleague Jo-Anne Pickel in file MB8-0002518 as a jurisprudential guide. This decision provides an in-depth interpretation of Article IE of the Refugee Convention. As a jurisprudential guide, its purpose is to set out the approach that must be followed in deciding on refugee protection claims based on this issue, and appeals thereof, in order to provide some consistency in decision-making within the RPD and the RAD.19 In the rest of my own analysis, I will use the approach that the decision proposes, as needed.

[20] In its decision, the RPD analyzed your testimony20 and the documentary evidence, specifically the resident cards for your wife and two of your children. They were issued in XXXX 2017 and are valid for a period of ten years, that is, until XXXX 2027. It came to the conclusion that, on a balance of probabilities, your wife and two of your minor children, who are citizens of the DRC, are permanent residents of the United States of America, a status that guarantees them rights equivalent to those enjoyed by citizens of that country. Having analyzed the various criteria that the loss of that status in the country can entail, it concluded that, on the final day of the hearing, your wife and your two children were still permanent residents of the United States, since you did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that their status had been cancelled by the US authorities.21
[21] In its decision, the RPD then focused on the presumption that the US authorities would be willing and able to protect you. It came to the conclusion that you had not rebutted that presumption.22

[22] According to my own analysis of your record, the RPD did not err as alleged when it found, on a balance of probabilities, that your wife and two of your children were still permanent residents of the United States of America on the final day of your hearing. At that time, in my opinion, it considered the relevant facts and law.23 The onus of showing that your wife and your two children had lost that status was clearly yours, and you did not do so.24 The existence of criteria that can lead to the loss of permanent resident status does not in itself give rise to the conclusion that, as a direct result, your wife and your two children did lose their status.25

[23] I will now refer to the principles applicable to your case, using the decision by my colleague Jo-Anne Pickel as my model. This has been designated as a jurisprudential guide in the approach to the analysis of a possible exclusion pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention:
- The appropriate date for assessing an appellant's status in their country of residence for the purpose of Article 1E of the Convention is the date of the RPD hearing.26
- Consideration must be given to the risk raised by claimants in respect of their country of residence prior to concluding that they are excluded from protection by the combined effect of Article 1E of the Convention and section 98 of the IRPA.27

[24] In your memorandum, you did not challenge the appropriate date for assessing your wife's permanent resident status in the United States, and that of two of your children, as the date of the RPD hearing. Nor did you challenge the RPD's conclusion in relation to the unrebutted presumption that the US authorities would be willing and able to protect your wife and your two children.

[25] As I indicated earlier, there is no basis for the argument in your memorandum that it was up to the Minister's representative to show that your wife and your two children still had permanent resident status in the United States.

[26] The RPD concluded that your wife and two of your children are persons referred to in Article 1E of the Refugee Convention, within the meaning of section 98 of the IRPA. This was not an error, in my opinion. The RPD did not have to analyze their claims in terms of their country of citizenship, the DRC, because that section itself makes it clear that they cannot be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
Applicability of section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and your credibility

[27] In its decision, the RPD identified a number of omissions, contradictions and implausibilities, not to mention behaviour inconsistent with that of a person who is being persecuted or who fears for his life. This led it to find that you were not a credible witness.28

[28] According to my own analysis of your record, in assessing your credibility, the RPD did not focus on useless details rather than the major issues. Nor did it set traps for you with the goal of rejecting your claim for refugee protection. It did not lack impartiality.

[29] Personally, I am of the opinion that the omissions, contradictions and implausibilities that the RPD identified clearly arose from the testimony you gave at the hearing and the documentary evidence you submitted. They deal with important aspects of your refugee protection claim. Let me give you an example. You testified about allegedly being the victim of an abduction in XXXX outside the XXXX XXXX in Kinshasa, ordered by the XXXX of the OGEFREM, about the time when you allegedly filed a complaint about it with the police, and about the follow-up to that complaint. You then contradicted yourself about your use of time, in that you were either at home for XXXX days or that you were in hospital. Then you ended up stating that your father took you to the hospital after the abduction. You contradicted yourself again a few seconds later when you stated that your father insisted that the police should see what had happened to you before you arrived at the hospital.29 It is clear to me that, not only did you contradict yourself, but your testimony also clearly changed with each statement you made.

[30] According to my own analysis of your record, the RPD did not err in any way when it found that the credibility of your allegations was seriously undermined by a number of omissions, contradictions and implausibilities.
Canada's constitutional and international obligations

[31] In your memorandum, you contend that, since you have no possibility of protection from the corrupt members of public institutions in the DRC, Canada would be in clear violation of its constitutional and international obligations if the RPD's determination is confirmed. With all respect, that argument has no merit.

[32] Actually, the argument is whether your potential deportation to the DRC would violate sections 7 and 12 of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms and our international obligations. It must be stated at this point that neither the RPD decision, nor my own decision, are about your deportation. They are only about whether you are a refugee or a person in need of protection within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.30 In this case, I see no exceptional circumstances that would give me cause to analyze a constitutional issue.31
CONCLUSION
[33] For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's decision to reject your refugee protection claims.

[34] Your appeal is dismissed.
(signed)
Alain Bissonnette
Me Alain Bissonnette
May 24, 2021
